title: The Typewriter of Valparaíso
premise: In 1973 Valparaíso, Rafael Okonkwo, a Nigerian-born driver for a prominent suffragist widow, secretly reads the letters he delivers and keeps a private ledger of what he learns. When a child is abandoned at his door with instructions to forget her face, Rafael discovers she is evidence of disappearances the new regime wants erased, and that his employer's correspondence is entangled in it. Racing a censor's typewriter that rewrites history as fast as it is recorded, Rafael must smuggle the truth into print before the century turns, sacrificing his anonymity, his safety, and finally his place in Chile. The book ends with him publishing under a dead man's name, alive but officially nonexistent, having traded identity itself for the record.
about_author: Ines Eastwick is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing confiscated letters from South American dictatorships. She writes from a coastal town where, she claims, every second house once hid a printing press.

chapters.title: The Weight of Letters
chapters.summary: Rafael Okonkwo drives Doña Amparo through Valparaíso's hills, reading her mail by lamplight each night and recording names in his private ledger. His POV establishes his double life: invisible servant, secret witness. Emotional beat: quiet pride curdling into unease as one letter mentions a name he has seen twice before.

chapters.title: Orders Come at Dawn
chapters.summary: Soldiers seal the port; Doña Amparo burns three letters before Rafael can read them, an act of trust or warning. Through his eyes we feel the city contract. Emotional beat: the first taste of fear, and the realization that his employer knows more than she says.

chapters.title: A Child at the Door
chapters.summary: A girl of six appears on Rafael's step with a note: forget this face. He hides her in the coal cellar, lying fluently for the first time in his life. Emotional beat: terror transformed into fierce, irrational protectiveness.

chapters.title: Doña Amparo's Silence
chapters.summary: Rafael tests his employer with a fabricated letter; her reaction reveals she recognizes the child. Her POV chapter shows a suffragist who won battles and lost herself, now calculating whether Rafael is asset or liability. Emotional beat: mutual suspicion sharpening into grudging alliance.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Names
chapters.summary: Rafael cross-references his years of stolen readings and finds a pattern: the disappeared all passed through one office above the customs house. Emotional beat: the intoxicating, dangerous thrill of seeing structure in chaos.

chapters.title: The Man Who Types
chapters.summary: Introduced through intercepted correspondence: Censor Vega, whose typewriter produces 'corrected' histories of the missing. His POV reveals a bureaucrat who believes order is mercy. Emotional beat: chilling calm; the antagonist is not cruel but convinced.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Raids begin on the hills. Rafael packs one bag per contingency, teaching the girl, Lucía, to memorize faces instead of trusting papers. Emotional beat: tenderness under pressure; survival as a discipline of love.

chapters.title: The Widow's Confession
chapters.summary: Doña Amparo admits the child is her granddaughter, daughter of a son who vanished after joining the resistance. She asks Rafael to become the family's memory. Emotional beat: grief finally spoken aloud, binding them.

chapters.title: Ink Under the Skin
chapters.summary: Rafael copies his ledger onto rice paper sewn into his coat lining, then burns the original. Vega's men search the house and find nothing—because Vega suspects everything. Emotional beat: the strange freedom of having nothing left to lose.

chapters.title: The Printer's Grave
chapters.summary: Seeking a press, Rafael contacts an exiled printer living as a dead man, who agrees to help only if the book carries no true names—including Rafael's. Emotional beat: the first explicit price of survival named aloud.

chapters.title: Vega's Archive
chapters.summary: Vega tours his warehouse of confiscated letters, restoring 'accuracy' to the historical record. He learns of a driver who reads mail and begins closing the net. Emotional beat: dread; the hunter is patient and methodical.

chapters.title: Lucía Speaks
chapters.summary: The girl breaks her silence and describes the room where she last saw her father—details matching Rafael's ledger exactly. Emotional beat: a child's testimony becoming the story's beating heart.

chapters.title: Betrayal in the Market
chapters.summary: A neighbor sells information; soldiers nearly take Lucía at the fish market, saved only by strangers' quick lies. Rafael realizes the network of protectors is also a web of potential informers. Emotional beat: paranoia corroding trust.

chapters.title: The Suffragist's Last Letter
chapters.summary: Doña Amparo writes openly to foreign journalists, choosing martyrdom over silence, and asks Rafael to deliver the letter he was never meant to read. Emotional beat: her agency reclaimed; his role reversed from thief to courier of truth.

chapters.title: Arrest
chapters.summary: Doña Amparo is taken. Vega interrogates Rafael, offering erasure of his own precarious immigration status in exchange for the child. Emotional beat: temptation laid bare—the regime offers him survival at the exact price of his soul.

chapters.title: The Typewriter's Rhythm
chapters.summary: Inside the customs house, Vega types the official account of Amparo's death while Rafael, released as bait, watches the office windows and maps the archive. Emotional beat: cold fury crystallizing into plan.

chapters.title: Stealing the Record
chapters.summary: Rafael and the printer infiltrate the archive during a blackout, swapping Vega's corrected pages for the true ones and photographing the originals. Emotional beat: exhilaration and near-catastrophe when Lucía, smuggled along as the only living witness, is almost seen.

chapters.title: What the Victors Will Write
chapters.summary: Vega discovers the substitution and understands history slipped through his fingers; he burns the warehouse rather than admit it. His POV cracks—he begins typing corrections no one will ever read. Emotional beat: power revealed as its own corruption, devouring its believer.

chapters.title: The Century Turns
chapters.summary: New Year's Eve 1979: the true account reaches foreign presses under a dead man's byline. Doña Amparo's letter is quoted worldwide; the disappeared have names again. Emotional beat: triumph shadowed by everything it cost.

chapters.title: Forget This Face
chapters.summary: Rafael puts Lucía on a boat to safety with adoptive parents, obeying the original instruction at last—forgetting her face so hers can survive. Emotional beat: heartbreak as the final act of protection.

chapters.title: A Man Without Papers
chapters.summary: Officially nonexistent, Rafael boards a northbound freighter. In his coat, the rice-paper ledger remains; in his mind, every name. Emotional beat: exile accepted as the fee already paid.

chapters.title: The Reader of Letters
chapters.summary: Decades later, an old man in Lagos receives a letter from a grown woman signing herself only 'the face you forgot.' He reads it twice, as he read everything, and answers. Emotional beat: grace—the record kept, the self surrendered, love outlasting both.
